lessons.title: Preventive Maintenance Schedules for African Work Conditions
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 1. In this lesson we focus on building and running a preventive maintenance schedule that actually works in African operating environments. Most machinery failures on the continent are not caused by bad machines. They are caused by dust, heat, poor fuel quality, bad roads, long supply chains and operators who were never trained to look after equipment. A good preventive maintenance schedule is your first line of defence and your cheapest insurance. The goal is simple: fix small problems before they become expensive breakdowns that stop your revenue. Start by creating an equipment register. For every machine you own or manage, record the make, model, year, serial number, engine type, rated capacity, fuel consumption, and the date it entered service. Then list every component that wears: filters, belts, hoses, tyres, tracks, hydraulic lines, batteries, brake pads, cutting edges, bearings and lubricants. For each component, note the manufacturer recommended service interval, then adjust it for your reality. If the manual says change the air filter every 500 hours in clean conditions, in a dusty quarry or on a dry season construction site you should cut that to 250 hours or even 150 hours. Heat is another killer. In ambient temperatures above 35 degrees Celsius, engine oil and hydraulic fluid break down faster, coolant systems work harder, and batteries lose water. Reduce oil change intervals by 20 to 30 percent in hot climates. Fuel quality across many African markets varies widely. Water, dirt and sulphur in diesel destroy injectors and fuel pumps. Install a water separator and a secondary fuel filter, and drain water traps daily. Buy fuel from trusted suppliers and let it settle before use. Store fuel in clean tanks with filters on the outlet. Build a maintenance calendar that fits your operation. Daily checks: engine oil level, coolant level, fuel level, hydraulic oil level, tyre pressure or track tension, lights, horn, brakes, and any visible leaks. These take ten minutes and prevent most roadside breakdowns. Weekly checks: battery terminals, fan belts, air filter condition, grease points, radiator fins, and tyre wear. Monthly checks: change engine oil and filters if running high hours, inspect hoses and clamps, test safety systems, check brake fluid, and clean the radiator. Annual or 2000-hour service: major inspection, valve clearance, injector testing, hydraulic system flush, transmission service, and structural inspection. Assign responsibility. Every machine must have a named operator and a named mechanic. The operator does daily checks and reports defects. The mechanic does scheduled services and repairs. The supervisor verifies that the work was done and signs the logbook. Keep a simple paper or phone-based logbook for each machine. Record date, hours, work done, parts used, cost, and the name of the person who did the work. This record helps you plan budgets, prove machine condition to buyers, and identify repeat failures. Spare parts planning is critical in Africa because delivery can take weeks. Keep a critical spares kit for each machine type: filters, belts, hoses, seals, fuses, bulbs, brake pads, and a set of hand tools. For high-value machines, keep a spare starter, alternator, water pump and injector set. Work with local suppliers and negotiate credit terms. Where possible, standardise your fleet so parts fit more than one machine. Train your operators. A trained operator hears a strange noise, feels a vibration, or sees a warning light and stops the machine before damage spreads. An untrained operator keeps pushing until the engine seizes. Run short toolbox talks every week on one topic: checking oil, greasing, tyre care, or safe shutdown. Finally, measure performance. Track mean time between failures, cost per hour, and availability percentage. If a machine is failing every month, the problem is not the machine. It is the maintenance system. Fix the system and the machine will reward you with more working hours and more profit. Remember, in African conditions, preventive maintenance is not a luxury. It is the difference between a business that grows and a business that spends all its money on repairs. Do the small things daily, and the big breakdowns will stay away.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Diesel Engines and Fuel Systems
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 2. Diesel engines power most of the machinery used across Africa: generators, trucks, excavators, tractors, pumps and boats. When a diesel engine fails, the whole operation stops. This lesson gives you a practical troubleshooting method that any mechanic or operator can follow. The first rule is to think in systems. A diesel engine needs four things to run: clean fuel, clean air, compression, and correct timing. If any one of these is missing, the engine will not start or will run badly. Start with the easiest checks before you open anything. Check the fuel level and the fuel shut-off valve. Many no-start problems are simply an empty tank or a closed valve. Check the battery voltage and terminals. A diesel engine needs a strong battery to turn the starter and to open the fuel solenoid. If the engine turns slowly, charge or replace the battery and clean the terminals. Check the air filter. A blocked air filter causes black smoke, low power and high fuel consumption. Remove it and inspect it in good light. If you cannot see light through it, replace it. Never run an engine without an air filter in dusty conditions. Check the fuel filters. Water and dirt in diesel are common in Africa. Drain the water separator daily. Replace fuel filters at the recommended interval or sooner if fuel quality is poor. If the engine starts then dies, suspect air in the fuel system. Bleed the system according to the manufacturer procedure. Now move to symptoms. Engine will not start: check battery, fuel supply, fuel solenoid, glow plugs or heater, and compression. If the engine turns over but does not fire, loosen a high-pressure injector line and crank the engine. If fuel pulses out, the injection pump is delivering fuel. If not, the problem is in the pump, the lift pump, or the fuel supply. Engine starts but runs rough: suspect air in the fuel, a clogged injector, a faulty injector, or low compression in one cylinder. Do a cylinder cut-out test. Loosen one injector line at a time. If the engine note does not change when you loosen a particular cylinder, that cylinder is not working. Engine lacks power: check air filter, fuel filters, turbocharger boost, exhaust blockage, and injector condition. Black smoke means too much fuel or not enough air. Blue smoke means burning oil, often worn rings or valve guides. White smoke means unburnt fuel, often cold engine, bad injectors, or low compression. Engine overheats: check coolant level, radiator fins for dust and mud, fan belt tension, thermostat, water pump, and radiator cap. In dusty African conditions, clean the radiator with compressed air or water every week. Do not open a hot radiator cap. Engine uses too much oil: check for leaks, worn rings, worn valve guides, or a blocked crankcase breather. Engine knocks: stop the engine immediately. A knock can mean a worn bearing, a loose flywheel, or incorrect injection timing. Continuing to run a knocking engine destroys the crankshaft and block. Fuel system care is especially important in Africa. Diesel is often contaminated with water, dirt and bacteria. Store fuel in clean tanks, allow it to settle, and filter it before use. Use a water separator and a primary filter with a transparent bowl so you can see water and dirt. Change filters regularly. Never use petrol in a diesel engine. Never use dirty containers to carry diesel. When working on a fuel system, keep everything spotlessly clean. Dirt entering an injector or injection pump causes expensive damage. Use clean rags, clean tools, and cap all open lines. For electronic diesel engines, you need a diagnostic scanner. Many modern machines have sensors for fuel pressure, rail pressure, camshaft position, and exhaust temperature. A scanner reads fault codes and saves hours of guessing. If you do not have a scanner, learn to check sensor wiring and connectors for corrosion and loose pins. Keep a notebook of fault codes and solutions. Build a troubleshooting kit: multimeter, fuel pressure gauge, compression tester, injector puller, torque wrench, feeler gauges, and a good torch. Train your team to use these tools correctly. Finally, document every repair. Record the symptom, the tests done, the cause found, and the fix applied. Over time, your records become the most valuable troubleshooting tool you own. In African workshops, experience is king, but documented experience is gold. Use it to train new mechanics and to reduce downtime on every machine you run.

lessons.title: Hydraulic Systems: Operation, Maintenance and Repair
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 3. Hydraulic systems power excavators, loaders, tractors, cranes, presses, and many other machines used in African construction, mining and agriculture. Hydraulics are powerful and reliable, but they are also sensitive to dirt, heat and poor maintenance. This lesson covers how hydraulic systems work, how to maintain them, and how to troubleshoot common faults. A basic hydraulic system has a reservoir, a pump, valves, hoses, cylinders, and a motor or actuator. The pump pushes oil through the system. Valves control direction, pressure and flow. Cylinders convert oil pressure into linear force. Motors convert oil pressure into rotation. Oil is the blood of the system. It transmits power, lubricates moving parts, and carries heat away. If the oil is dirty, hot, or low, the system will fail. Start with the reservoir. Check the oil level daily with the machine on level ground and the cylinders retracted. Use the correct oil grade as specified by the manufacturer. Do not mix different oil brands or grades. Check the breather cap. A blocked breather causes pressure build-up and oil leaks. Clean or replace it regularly. Check the suction strainer and return filter. Replace them at the recommended interval. In dusty conditions, replace them sooner. Inspect hoses and fittings every week. Look for cracks, bulges, chafing, and leaks. A pinhole leak in a high-pressure hose can inject oil into your skin, which is a medical emergency. Never use your hand to search for leaks. Use a piece of cardboard or paper. Replace any damaged hose immediately. Do not try to patch a hydraulic hose. Check cylinder rods for scratches, dents and rust. A damaged rod destroys the seals and causes leaks. Keep rods clean and wipe them with a clean cloth. Check for drift. If a cylinder slowly moves under load, the seals are worn or the control valve is leaking. Check the hydraulic oil temperature. Normal operating temperature is usually between 50 and 80 degrees Celsius. If the oil gets too hot, it breaks down, seals harden, and the system loses power. Causes of overheating include low oil level, blocked cooler, wrong oil, continuous relief valve operation, or a worn pump. Clean the oil cooler with compressed air or water. In African heat, this is a weekly job. Now troubleshooting. Slow operation: check oil level, filter blockage, pump wear, relief valve setting, and cylinder seals. If all functions are slow, suspect the pump or the relief valve. If one function is slow, suspect that circuit valve or cylinder. No movement: check oil level, pump drive coupling, relief valve, and control linkage. Listen for the pump. A healthy pump makes a steady sound. A whining or growling pump may be cavitating due to low oil, a blocked suction strainer, or air in the system. Bleed air from the system after any repair. Excessive heat: check cooler, oil level, relief valve, and internal leakage. Contaminated oil: look for milky oil, which means water. Look for metal particles, which mean internal wear. Look for black oil, which means overheating or seal breakdown. If oil is contaminated, drain the system, flush it, replace filters, and refill with clean oil. Find and fix the source of contamination. Water enters through damaged breathers, condensation, or washing with a pressure washer. Dirt enters through dirty tools, open lines, or dirty oil. Repairing hydraulic components requires cleanliness. Work in a clean area. Wash the machine before opening anything. Cap all open lines and ports. Use lint-free rags. Torque all fittings to specification. Replace all O-rings and seals that you disturb. Never reuse a seal. When replacing a pump or motor, check the drive coupling and alignment. Misalignment causes rapid failure. When replacing a cylinder, bleed the air and check for smooth operation through the full stroke. Keep a hydraulic repair kit: seal kits, O-rings, hoses, fittings, couplings, filters, and the correct oil. Train your operators to report leaks, unusual noises, slow functions, and hot oil immediately. A small leak today becomes a major failure tomorrow. In African operations, hydraulic downtime is expensive because parts may be far away. Preventive care and quick, clean repairs keep your machines working and your business profitable. Remember, hydraulics reward cleanliness and punish neglect. Keep it clean, keep it cool, and keep it working.

lessons.title: Electrical Systems and Fault Finding on Heavy Machinery
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 4. Electrical faults are among the most common reasons machinery stops working in African workshops and job sites. Batteries go flat, alternators fail, wiring corrodes, and starters burn out. This lesson teaches you how to understand basic electrical systems on heavy machinery and how to find and fix faults safely and quickly. Safety first. Electricity can kill. Always disconnect the battery before working on electrical systems. Remove the negative terminal first and connect it last. Wear insulated gloves and use insulated tools. Never work alone on high-voltage systems. If a machine has a high-voltage hybrid or electric drive, do not touch it unless you are trained and authorised. A basic machine electrical system has a battery, an alternator, a starter, fuses, relays, switches, wiring, sensors, and a control unit. The battery stores energy. The alternator charges the battery while the engine runs. The starter turns the engine. Fuses protect circuits from overload. Relays switch high current using low current. Switches and sensors send signals. The control unit makes decisions. Start with the battery. Check the voltage with a multimeter. A fully charged 12-volt battery should read about 12.6 volts with the engine off. A 24-volt system should read about 25.2 volts. If the reading is below 12.2 or 24.4 volts, charge the battery. Check the terminals for corrosion. Clean them with a wire brush and apply petroleum jelly. Check the battery hold-down. A loose battery can crack and fail. Check the electrolyte level in serviceable batteries and top up with distilled water only. Check the charging system. Start the engine and measure battery voltage. It should rise to about 13.8 to 14.4 volts for a 12-volt system, or 27.6 to 28.8 volts for a 24-volt system. If the voltage does not rise, the alternator or the regulator is faulty. Check the alternator belt tension and condition. A loose or glazed belt slips and does not charge. Check the wiring from the alternator to the battery. Look for loose or corroded connections. Check the starter system. If the engine does not crank, check the battery, the starter relay, the ignition switch, the neutral safety switch, and the starter motor. Use a multimeter to check for voltage at the starter solenoid when the key is turned. If voltage is present but the starter does not turn, the starter is faulty. If voltage is not present, trace the circuit back to the switch or relay. Check fuses and relays. A blown fuse is a symptom, not a cause. Find out why the fuse blew. A short circuit or an overloaded circuit will blow the new fuse too. Keep a supply of correct-rated fuses. Never use a higher-rated fuse or a piece of wire to bypass a fuse. That causes fires. Check wiring and connectors. In African conditions, heat, dust, moisture and vibration damage wiring. Look for cracked insulation, broken wires, corroded pins, and loose connectors. Use a wiring diagram. If you do not have one, get one. Trace circuits methodically. Do not guess. Check grounds. A bad ground causes many strange faults. Clean and tighten all ground connections. Add a star washer for good contact. Check sensors and control units. Modern machines use sensors for engine speed, temperature, pressure, position and flow. A faulty sensor sends wrong signals and the machine runs badly or stops. Use a diagnostic scanner to read fault codes. If you do not have a scanner, check sensor resistance and wiring according to the manufacturer specification. Keep a good multimeter, a test light, a wire stripper, crimping tool, heat shrink, and a supply of wire and connectors. Label wires when you disconnect them. Take photos before you start. Work systematically. Divide the system into circuits and test one circuit at a time. Do not replace parts randomly. Test first, then replace. Common faults in Africa include flat batteries due to short trips and poor charging, corroded terminals due to humidity and dust, damaged wiring due to rodents and vibration, and failed alternators due to dust and heat. Prevent these by keeping the battery clean and charged, protecting wiring with conduit, sealing connectors, and cleaning the alternator cooling vents. Train operators to report electrical symptoms early: dim lights, slow cranking, warning lights, burning smells, and intermittent faults. Intermittent faults are the hardest to find. They often come from loose connections or broken wires inside insulation. Wiggle test the harness while watching the multimeter. Finally, document every electrical repair. Record the fault, the tests, the cause, and the fix. Build a library of wiring diagrams and fault codes for every machine you run. In African workshops, electrical skills are scarce and valuable. Master them and you become the person everyone calls when machines stop. Stay safe, work clean, and test before you replace.

lessons.title: Starting a Machinery Repair Business in Africa
lessons.body: Welcome to Module 7, Lesson 5. This lesson is about turning your technical skills into a profitable machinery repair business. Across Africa, there is huge demand for reliable mechanics, welders, electricians and machine operators. Roads, farms, mines, construction sites and factories all need machines, and machines always break down. If you can fix them quickly and honestly, you will never lack work. But technical skill alone is not enough. You need a business mindset. Start by defining your services. You could specialise in diesel engines, hydraulics, auto electrical, welding and fabrication, or general plant repair. Specialising helps you build a reputation and charge higher rates. You can also offer mobile services, going to the customer site with a fully equipped vehicle. Mobile service is powerful in Africa because many machines cannot move to a workshop. Next, understand your costs. List every cost: tools, fuel, transport, spare parts, rent, phone data, protective clothing, insurance, licences and taxes. Add your labour time. Calculate your hourly rate. A simple formula: add all monthly costs, add the profit you want, divide by the number of billable hours you can realistically work. Many mechanics undercharge because they forget hidden costs. Charge properly and explain your value. Register your business. In most African countries you need a business name registration, a tax number, and sometimes a trade licence. Registration helps you open a bank account, win contracts, and build trust with corporate clients. Keep records from day one. Use a simple cash book or a phone app. Record every sale, every expense, every part bought, and every payment received. Separate business money from personal money. This discipline prevents the common trap of a busy mechanic who has no money. Build a customer base. Start with the machines around you: farms, transport companies, construction sites, factories, hospitals, hotels and schools. Visit them. Introduce yourself. Offer a free basic inspection. Fix small problems well and on time. Word of mouth is the strongest marketing in Africa. One happy customer brings five more. Use WhatsApp and social media to show your work. Post before and after photos. Share simple maintenance tips. Respond quickly to messages. Keep your phone charged and your number active. Manage spare parts carefully. Parts are often the biggest cost and the biggest delay. Build relationships with suppliers in your country and abroad. Negotiate discounts for bulk buying. Keep a small stock of fast-moving parts: filters, belts, hoses, seals, bearings, fuses, bulbs and lubricants. For slow-moving or expensive parts, order only when you have a confirmed job and a deposit. Never use cheap counterfeit parts. They fail quickly, damage machines, and destroy your reputation. Invest in tools. Good tools save time and produce quality work. Start with the basics: socket sets, spanners, torque wrench, multimeter, compression tester, hydraulic jack, grease gun, welding machine, grinder, drill and hand tools. Buy quality tools gradually. Insure your tools and your vehicle. Train yourself continuously. Attend courses, watch reputable videos, read manuals, and learn from older mechanics. Join a professional association if one exists. Teach your apprentices properly. A trained apprentice becomes a valuable employee or partner. Manage your time and jobs. Use a job card for every repair. Record the customer name, machine details, complaint, diagnosis, parts used, labour, total cost, and payment status. Give the customer a copy. This prevents disputes and helps you track profitability per job. Handle money wisely. Take a deposit for parts. Invoice promptly. Follow up on debts politely but firmly. Keep a reserve for slow months. Reinvest in tools, transport and training. Avoid borrowing for consumption. Borrow only for assets that generate income. Stay legal and ethical. Give honest diagnoses. Do not replace parts that are still good. Do not overcharge. Respect safety rules. Dispose of used oil and batteries responsibly. Pay your taxes. These habits build a business that lasts. Finally, think growth. You can grow from a one-person mobile mechanic to a workshop with employees, then to a parts dealership, then to a training centre. Each step needs systems: job cards, stock records, staff roles, and customer follow-up. In Africa, the opportunity is enormous. Machines are everywhere, and good repair services are scarce. If you combine technical excellence with business discipline, you will build a profitable, respected and lasting enterprise that serves your community and creates jobs for others. Start today with the next machine that needs your help.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Machinery Repair Costing, Parts Sourcing and Downtime Control in Africa

For African machinery operators and repair enterprises, the difference between a profitable season and a loss-making one rarely comes down to technical skill alone. It comes down to how well you control three variables: the cost of parts, the cost of downtime, and the reliability of your supply chain. This practical reference lesson gives you the working numbers, sourcing routes, and record-keeping tools you need to run machinery repair as a business, not just a trade. Whether you service a single tractor on your own farm or run a workshop serving twenty clients across a district, the figures and frameworks below are drawn from real African operating conditions.

Why Costing Discipline Matters More Than Tooling

Many African repair businesses fail not because the mechanic cannot fix the machine, but because the business cannot price the job correctly. A 2021 study by the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA) found that small and medium agricultural machinery enterprises in sub-Saharan Africa operate on average at 12-18% net margin when they track costs properly, but many operate blind and unknowingly run at a loss on 30-40% of jobs. The fix is simple in principle: know your parts cost, your labour cost, your transport cost, and your downtime cost, and price with all four in view.

Parts sourcing is the single largest variable cost in most repair jobs, typically 45-65% of the invoice. Where you source determines both your margin and your customer's downtime. A genuine OEM part from a regional distributor may cost 40% more than a grey-market equivalent, but if it lasts three times longer and arrives in one week instead of six, the total cost of ownership is lower. Your job as a business is to make that trade-off visible to the customer, not to hide it.

Parts Sourcing Routes: A Practical Comparison

The table below compares the four main sourcing routes available to African machinery repair businesses. Figures are indicative ranges drawn from regional distributor pricing and logistics data; verify locally before quoting.

Sourcing Route Typical Lead Time Price Index (OEM = 100) Warranty Best For
OEM authorised distributor (regional) 1-3 weeks 100 12 months Critical engine, hydraulic, transmission parts
Aftermarket quality brand (e.g. equivalent-tier) 3-10 days 55-75 3-6 months Filters, belts, bearings, seals
Local market / used parts dealer Same day 20-45 None Non-critical brackets, panels, older machines
Direct import (Alibaba, eBay, specialist) 4-12 weeks 30-60 + freight & duty Variable Bulk consumables, planned rebuilds

Price index and lead-time ranges compiled from regional distributor quotes and AGRA (2021) "Africa Agriculture Status Report" logistics data. Freight and duty can add 25-60% to direct import landed cost.

Downtime Cost: The Number Most Businesses Ignore

Downtime is the hidden invoice. When a customer's tractor fails during land preparation, the loss is not just the repair bill, it is the hectares not planted, the labour idle, and the season window closing. Quantifying this lets you justify premium pricing for fast response and lets your customer see the real value of preventive maintenance.

Machine / Operation Typical Daily Output Estimated Downtime Cost (USD/day) Peak Season Multiplier
75-100 hp tractor + plough 4-8 ha/day 150-400 1.5-2.5x
Combine harvester (small-medium) 8-20 ha/day 400-1,200 2-4x
Diesel irrigation pump (10-30 hp) Irrigates 1-4 ha/day 80-300 (crop loss risk) 3-5x in dry spell
Maize sheller / thresher 5-15 t/day 100-350 2-3x at harvest
Feed mixer / hammer mill 2-8 t/day 60-250 1.5-2x

Downtime cost estimates derived from ILRI livestock feed and mechanisation studies and FAO farm machinery cost-of-ownership frameworks. Actual figures vary by crop, region, and season.

⚠ SAFETY WARNING â DIESEL, HYDRAULIC FLUID AND BATTERY HANDLING

Diesel fuel, hydraulic oil, and battery electrolyte are hazardous. Diesel and hydraulic fluid are skin irritants and suspected carcinogens with prolonged exposure; never siphon fuel by mouth. Battery electrolyte (sulphuric acid) causes severe burns and can blind on contact with eyes. Always wear nitrile gloves, chemical splash goggles, and long sleeves when handling fluids. Work in ventilated areas only â diesel exhaust and battery charging fumes (hydrogen) are toxic and explosive. Store fluids away from open flame and out of reach of children and animals. In case of eye or skin contact with electrolyte, flush with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Dispose of used oil and filters through licensed collectors â never pour onto soil or into waterways. These precautions align with WHO chemical safety guidance and national occupational health regulations.

Building Your Repair Business Around the Numbers

With the cost drivers and sourcing routes above, you can construct a simple job costing sheet that protects your margin on every job. The formula is:

Job Price = Parts Cost + Labour Hours Ã Rate + Transport + Downtime Premium + Overhead + Margin

Two practical rules separate profitable African repair businesses from struggling ones. First, never quote a job without a 15% contingency for parts price movement and unexpected findings â currency volatility and supply disruptions are normal, not exceptional. Second, always offer the customer a preventive maintenance contract alongside the repair. A contract that delivers scheduled servicing at a fixed monthly fee converts unpredictable repair income into predictable recurring revenue, and it reduces the customer's downtime cost by 40-60% according to FAO mechanisation studies.

For parts, build relationships with two suppliers per critical category â one regional distributor for genuine parts and one aftermarket supplier for fast-moving consumables. Keep a minimum stock of high-failure items (filters, belts, hoses, seals, injector washers, hydraulic fittings) because these account for 60-70% of field breakdowns and can be resolved same-day if stock is on hand. The capital tied up in a $500-$2,000 consumables stock is recovered many times over in reduced downtime and faster job turnaround.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Cost every job before quoting: parts + labour + transport + overhead + 15% contingency + margin.
  • Maintain two suppliers per critical part category â one OEM/regional, one aftermarket â to avoid single-source failure.
  • Stock the top 20 fast-moving consumables (filters, belts, hoses, seals, fittings) to enable same-day repair.
  • Quantify customer downtime in hectares or tonnes lost, and use it to justify premium response pricing.
  • Offer a preventive maintenance contract at a fixed monthly fee to convert repair income into recurring revenue.
  • Record every repair: machine hours, failure mode, parts used, labour hours, and cost â this data drives better pricing and parts forecasting.
  • Handle all fluids and batteries with PPE and dispose of used oil and filters through licensed collectors only.
  • Review your parts price index quarterly against currency and freight movements, and adjust your quotes accordingly.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Farm Power and Machinery (Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization resource portal): https://www.fao.org/sustainable-agricultural-mechanization
  • FAO â Agricultural Engineering and Farm Machinery publications and cost-of-ownership tools: https://www.fao.org/publications
  • ILRI â Livestock and Irrigation Value Chains for Ethiopian Smallholders (LIVES) and mechanisation research: https://www.ilri.org
  • AGRA â Africa Agriculture Status Report (annual, includes mechanisation and agribusiness finance data): https://agra.org
  • WHO â Chemical Safety and Occupational Health guidance for fuel, oil, and battery handling: https://www.who.int/health-topics/chemical-safety

quiz.q: Which document should be consulted first before performing any repair on a machine?
quiz.explanation: The manufacturer service manual gives approved procedures, torque values, and safety warnings specific to the machine.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of lockout tagout during machinery repair?
options: C) To prevent unexpected energization or startup
quiz.explanation: Lockout tagout isolates energy sources so the machine cannot start or release stored energy while work is in progress.

quiz.q: Which condition most often indicates a failing bearing in rotating machinery?
options: A) Bright paint on the housing
B) A clean oil sight glass
quiz.explanation: Worn or damaged bearings typically produce increased vibration, growling noise, and heat before complete failure.

quiz.q: What is the correct action if a machine guard must be removed for repair?
options: A) Replace it before returning the machine to service
B) Leave it off until the next shift
C) Store it in the tool crib indefinitely
D) Paint it and reinstall later
quiz.explanation: Guards are safety devices and must be reinstalled and verified before the machine is returned to operation.

quiz.q: Why should hydraulic system pressure be relieved before disconnecting lines?
options: B) To prevent high pressure fluid injection injury
quiz.explanation: Trapped hydraulic pressure can cause sudden fluid release and serious injection injuries, so it must be relieved first.

quiz.q: Which measurement is used to check whether a shaft is bent or out of alignment?
quiz.explanation: A dial indicator measures runout and helps identify bent shafts, misalignment, or coupling problems.

quiz.q: What should be done with used oil and contaminated rags after maintenance?
options: A) Burn them in the shop
B) Pour oil down a drain
C) Dispose of them according to environmental regulations
D) Mix them with regular trash
quiz.explanation: Used oil and contaminated materials require proper handling and disposal under environmental and workplace regulations.

quiz.q: What is the best way to verify a repair was successful before full production?
options: A) Ask a coworker to guess
B) Skip testing to save time
D) Perform a controlled test run and inspect readings
quiz.explanation: A controlled test run with checks of temperature, vibration, pressure, and function confirms the repair is safe and effective.

quiz.q: In many African work environments, what is the most common cause of accelerated machinery wear?
quiz.explanation: Dust and high temperatures accelerate wear on filters, belts, and lubricants, so maintenance intervals must be shortened.

quiz.q: When adapting a preventive maintenance schedule to African conditions, which interval should usually be shortened?
quiz.explanation: Dust and heat degrade engine oil faster, so oil change intervals should be shortened compared to temperate climates.

quiz.q: Which daily check is especially important before starting machinery on a dusty African site?
quiz.explanation: A clogged air filter causes poor combustion and engine damage, so it must be checked daily in dusty conditions.

quiz.q: A diesel engine cranks but does not start. Which is the most likely fuel system fault?
options: A) Air in the fuel lines
quiz.explanation: Air in the fuel system prevents proper injection and is a common cause of no-start conditions in diesel engines.

quiz.q: Black smoke from a diesel exhaust usually indicates what problem?
options: A) Over-fueling or restricted air intake
quiz.explanation: Excess fuel or insufficient air causes incomplete combustion and black smoke.

quiz.q: What is the primary function of a diesel fuel injector?
options: A) Atomize fuel into the combustion chamber
quiz.explanation: Injectors atomize fuel so it mixes with air and burns efficiently.

quiz.q: In a hydraulic system, what does a relief valve do?
quiz.explanation: The relief valve protects the system by limiting pressure to a safe maximum.

quiz.q: Hydraulic oil that appears milky usually indicates what?
quiz.explanation: Milky hydraulic oil indicates water contamination, which reduces lubrication and can damage components.

quiz.q: Which component creates flow in a hydraulic system?
quiz.explanation: The pump converts mechanical energy into hydraulic flow, driving the system.

quiz.q: A hydraulic cylinder drifts slowly under load. What is a likely cause?
options: A) Internal leakage past the piston seal
quiz.explanation: Internal seal leakage allows fluid to bypass the piston, causing drift.

quiz.q: Which electrical fault causes a heavy machinery starter to click but not crank?
quiz.explanation: Low battery voltage or high resistance in cables causes the solenoid to click without cranking the engine.

quiz.q: What is the correct first step when troubleshooting an electrical fault on heavy machinery?
options: A) Check battery voltage and connections
quiz.explanation: Verifying battery voltage and clean, tight connections is the logical first step before replacing parts.

quiz.q: Which instrument is best for checking continuity in a machine wiring harness?
quiz.explanation: A multimeter set to continuity or resistance tests whether a circuit is complete.

quiz.q: When starting a machinery repair business in Africa, what is a key first step?
options: A) Identify a specific local market need
B) Buy the most expensive tools
C) Import all parts from Europe
quiz.explanation: Understanding local demand for specific repairs helps focus services and investment.

quiz.q: Why is building relationships with local parts suppliers important for a repair business?
options: A) It reduces downtime and improves parts availability
D) It removes the need for tools
quiz.explanation: Reliable suppliers help source parts quickly, reducing customer downtime and improving reputation.

quiz.q: Which pricing strategy is often suitable for a new machinery repair business?
options: A) Competitive pricing based on local rates
quiz.explanation: Studying local market rates helps set competitive prices that attract customers while covering costs.

quiz.q: What should be included in a preventive maintenance record for each machine?
options: A) Date, tasks done, parts replaced, and hours
quiz.explanation: Detailed records help track machine history, plan future maintenance, and prove service quality.

quiz.q: Which safety precaution is essential before repairing a hydraulic system?
quiz.explanation: Trapped hydraulic pressure can cause serious injury, so it must be released before work begins.

quiz.q: Why should coolant be checked more often in hot African climates?
options: A) Higher temperatures increase evaporation and overheating risk
quiz.explanation: Heat increases evaporation and demands on the cooling system, so coolant levels and concentration must be monitored.

quiz.q: A machine alternator warning light stays on. What should be checked first?
options: A) Alternator belt tension and connections
quiz.explanation: A loose or broken alternator belt and poor connections are common causes of charging system warnings.

quiz.q: What is a practical way to reduce dust intake on machinery in dry African conditions?
options: A) Use pre-cleaners and service air filters frequently
D) Use water in the fuel
quiz.explanation: Pre-cleaners and frequent air filter service reduce dust entering the engine and extend engine life.

quiz.q: Which document is most useful as a practical reference for a machinery repair technician?
quiz.explanation: Manufacturer service manuals provide specifications, torque values, and procedures specific to the machine.
